---
title: "Tagging words by grammatical function"
subtitle: "Read part-of-speech tags from a small trained model"
description: "Learn how a part-of-speech tagger labels workforce text and why held-out accuracy has limits."
categories: [word parsing, part-of-speech tagging, workforce research]
---

After sentence labeling, the team examines single words in a job posting.
It asks which words describe actions.

This changes the level of analysis. The team no longer classifies whole
sentences about training or schedules. It examines each word's grammatical
function.

A **part-of-speech tagger** assigns a grammatical tag to each token.
Tags can identify things, actions, descriptions, helper verbs, numbers, or
punctuation. This lesson uses a UDPipe tagger with 500 hand-labeled training
sentences from the Universal Dependencies English Web Treebank.
A **treebank** contains sentences with human-assigned word-level labels.

::: {.callout-note}
The author created the fictional Riverton Workforce Lab, its job board, and
its training flyer for teaching. The project includes local UDPipe model and
treebank files. The lesson downloads nothing during execution.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- describe common Universal POS tags in plain language.
- run a local UDPipe part-of-speech tagger on fixed tokens.
- examine a tagging mistake in a job-posting sentence.
- read a held-out accuracy score.
- explain why weblog-post accuracy does not establish accuracy on job postings.
:::

## Load the local files

In this read-only pass, readr opens files, and dplyr and tibble handle tables.
The purrr package processes token lists, tokenizers splits words, and udpipe
assigns tags. The digest package supplies file fingerprints for comparison.
The code reads the trained model from disk and records settings for the
bundled run. It does not train a model.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(tokenizers)
library(stringr)
library(udpipe)
library(digest)

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

learning_curve <- read_csv(
  "data/treebank/tagger-learning-curve.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    training_sentences = col_integer(),
    training_tokens = col_integer(),
    held_out_tokens = col_integer(),
    correct_tokens = col_integer(),
    accuracy = col_double()
  )
)

metadata <- read_csv(
  "data/treebank/treebank-metadata.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    artifact = col_character(),
    description = col_character(),
    source = col_character(),
    source_url = col_character(),
    retrieved_on = col_character(),
    license = col_character(),
    fingerprint = col_character()
  )
)

builder_script_path <- "data-raw/build-treebank-tagger.R"
builder_seed_match <- read_lines(builder_script_path) |>
  str_subset("^set.seed\\(") |>
  str_match("^set.seed\\((\\d+)\\)")
builder_seed <- as.integer(builder_seed_match[1, 2])
rng_settings <- RNGkind()

learning_curve_path <- "data/treebank/tagger-learning-curve.csv"
learning_curve_fingerprint <- digest(
  paste(read_lines(learning_curve_path), collapse = "\n"),
  algo = "sha256",
  serialize = FALSE
)
expected_curve_fingerprint <- metadata |>
  filter(artifact == "tagger-learning-curve.csv") |>
  pull(fingerprint)

metadata_display <- metadata |>
  filter(
    artifact %in% c(
      "en_ewt-train-excerpt.conllu",
      "en_ewt-held-out.conllu",
      "en_ewt-500-tagger.udpipe",
      "tagger-learning-curve.csv"
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(fingerprint_start = str_sub(fingerprint, 1, 12)) |>
  select(artifact, source, retrieved_on, license, fingerprint_start)

reproducibility_table <- tibble(
  item = c(
    "Builder seed from script",
    "Current R RNG kind",
    "Current normal generator",
    "Current sample generator",
    "Current R version"
  ),
  value = c(
    as.character(builder_seed),
    rng_settings[[1]],
    rng_settings[[2]],
    rng_settings[[3]],
    R.version.string
  )
)
```

## Tag fixed tokens

The model's training covers token tagging, not raw-text sentence splitting.
The code first tokenizes each Riverton text unit.
It writes one token per line and declares the input as vertical text to UDPipe.

The output contains a **lemma**, a word's dictionary form.
For example, `is` has the lemma `be`.
The shorthand `\(tokens)` defines an R function that handles one sentence's
tokens at a time.

```{r}
tagger <- udpipe_load_model(
  "data/treebank/en_ewt-500-tagger.udpipe"
)

vertical <- sentences$text |>
  tokenize_words(lowercase = FALSE, strip_punct = FALSE) |>
  map_chr(\(tokens) paste(tokens, collapse = "\n"))

tagged <- udpipe_annotate(
  tagger,
  x = vertical,
  doc_id = sentences$sentence_id,
  tokenizer = "vertical",
  tagger = "default",
  parser = "none"
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  as_tibble()

paid_sentence_tags <- tagged |>
  filter(doc_id == "s001") |>
  select(token, upos, lemma)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  paid_sentence_tags,
  col.names = c("Token", "POS tag", "Lemma"),
  caption = "Tags for 'Paid 12-week training is provided.'",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(tagged), 178L),
  identical(
    paid_sentence_tags$token,
    c("Paid", "12", "-", "week", "training", "is", "provided", ".")
  ),
  identical(
    paid_sentence_tags$upos,
    c("PROPN", "NUM", "PUNCT", "NOUN", "NOUN", "AUX", "VERB", "PUNCT")
  ),
  identical(
    paid_sentence_tags$lemma,
    c("Paid", "12", "-", "week", "training", "be", "provid", ".")
  )
)
```

The sentence has eight tokens after keeping punctuation. Two outputs are wrong
in a way a reader can judge. `Paid` is not a proper noun. It describes the
training, and the tagger likely followed the capital letter at the start of the
sentence. The lemma `provid` for `provided` is not a word. The model guessed a
stem from a suffix rule.

## Count the tags

The tagger uses **Universal POS tags**.
The **tagset** is its fixed list of permitted labels.

- `NOUN` marks things.
- `VERB` marks actions.
- `ADJ` marks descriptions.
- `ADP` marks words such as `of` and `in`.
- `AUX` marks helper verbs such as `is`.
- `DET` marks words such as `the` and `a`.
- `PART` marks particles such as `to` in `to apply`.
- `PROPN` marks names.
- `PRON` marks pronouns.
- `ADV` marks adverbs.
- `CCONJ` marks coordinating conjunctions such as `and`.
- `INTJ` marks interjections.

```{r}
tag_counts <- tagged |>
  count(upos, sort = TRUE)

punctuation_tokens <- sum(tagged$upos == "PUNCT")
tokens_without_punctuation <- nrow(tagged) - punctuation_tokens

intj_tokens <- tagged |>
  filter(upos == "INTJ") |>
  select(doc_id, token)

propn_tokens <- tagged |>
  filter(upos == "PROPN") |>
  select(doc_id, token)

expected_tag_counts <- tibble(
  upos = c(
    "NOUN",
    "PUNCT",
    "VERB",
    "AUX",
    "ADJ",
    "DET",
    "PROPN",
    "ADP",
    "NUM",
    "PART",
    "PRON",
    "ADV",
    "CCONJ",
    "INTJ"
  ),
  n = c(45L, 25L, 24L, 20L, 17L, 16L, 11L, 7L, 6L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tag_counts,
  col.names = c("POS tag", "Tagged tokens"),
  caption = "Universal POS tag counts across the 28 Riverton text units",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(tag_counts, expected_tag_counts),
  identical(punctuation_tokens, 25L),
  identical(tokens_without_punctuation, 153L),
  identical(intj_tokens$doc_id, "s002"),
  identical(intj_tokens$token, "No"),
  identical(
    propn_tokens$token,
    c(
      "Paid",
      "Clear",
      "RIVERTON",
      "SKILLS",
      "OPEN",
      "HOUSE",
      "DATA",
      "SUPPORT",
      "CERTIFICATE",
      "Paid",
      "October"
    )
  )
)
```

Nouns are the largest group, followed by punctuation, verbs, and helper verbs.
These categories provide a starting point for checks.
The first sentence's errors show that the table is not a perfect grammatical
description of the postings.

This lesson keeps punctuation and tags 178 tokens.
Removing the 25 `PUNCT` tokens leaves the 153 word tokens counted in Lesson 15.

The only `INTJ` is `No` in `s002`, which is wrong in context.
Seven of the 11 `PROPN` tokens are all-capital flyer words:
`RIVERTON`, `SKILLS`, `OPEN`, `HOUSE`, `DATA`, `SUPPORT`, and `CERTIFICATE`.
Two are sentence-initial `Paid` in `s001` and `s025`.
One is `Clear` in `s022`. The remaining token, `October` in `s028`, has the
correct tag.

The tagger treats capital letters as evidence of names.
An overall accuracy score does not show this systematic error on the Riverton
text.

## Read the accuracy number

This score is for 13 held-out political weblog posts from the same treebank, not
for job postings. **Held-out** means text kept back from training so it can be
reserved for scoring. The posts in both treebank excerpts are weblog
documents from 2003 to 2006, which strengthens the domain-transfer warning.

```{r}
train_path <- "data/treebank/en_ewt-train-excerpt.conllu"
held_out_path <- "data/treebank/en_ewt-held-out.conllu"

read_gold_tokens <- function(path) {
  udpipe_read_conllu(path) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    filter(!str_detect(token_id, "[^0-9]"), !is.na(upos))
}

train_newdoc_ids <- read_lines(train_path) |>
  str_subset(fixed("# newdoc id = ")) |>
  str_remove(fixed("# newdoc id = "))

held_newdoc_ids <- read_lines(held_out_path) |>
  str_subset(fixed("# newdoc id = ")) |>
  str_remove(fixed("# newdoc id = "))

treebank_years <- str_match(
  c(train_newdoc_ids, held_newdoc_ids),
  "_ENG_(\\d{4})"
)[, 2] |>
  as.integer()

train_gold <- read_gold_tokens(train_path) |>
  transmute(token, gold_upos = upos)

held <- read_gold_tokens(held_out_path) |>
  transmute(sentence_id, token, gold_upos = upos)

lookup <- train_gold |>
  count(token, gold_upos, name = "n") |>
  arrange(token, desc(n), gold_upos) |>
  group_by(token) |>
  slice(1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(token, baseline_upos = gold_upos)

held_vertical <- held |>
  group_by(sentence_id) |>
  summarise(text = paste(token, collapse = "\n"), .groups = "drop")

held_predictions <- udpipe_annotate(
  tagger,
  x = held_vertical$text,
  doc_id = held_vertical$sentence_id,
  tokenizer = "vertical",
  tagger = "default",
  parser = "none"
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(doc_id) |>
  mutate(token_row = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(
    sentence_id = doc_id,
    token_row,
    tagger_upos = upos
  )

scored <- held |>
  left_join(lookup, by = "token") |>
  mutate(
    baseline_upos = coalesce(baseline_upos, "NOUN"),
    seen_in_training = token %in% train_gold$token
  ) |>
  group_by(sentence_id) |>
  mutate(token_row = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(held_predictions, by = c("sentence_id", "token_row")) |>
  mutate(
    baseline_correct = baseline_upos == gold_upos,
    tagger_correct = tagger_upos == gold_upos,
    easy_gold_tag = gold_upos %in% c("PUNCT", "DET")
  )

scored_500 <- learning_curve |>
  filter(training_sentences == 500L) |>
  mutate(
    calculated_accuracy = correct_tokens / held_out_tokens,
    accuracy_percent = round(calculated_accuracy * 100, 2)
  )

learning_curve_display <- learning_curve |>
  mutate(
    accuracy_percent = round(accuracy * 100, 2)
  )

gain_100_to_500 <- learning_curve |>
  filter(training_sentences %in% c(100L, 500L)) |>
  summarise(
    points = diff(accuracy) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pull(points)

gain_500_to_2000 <- learning_curve |>
  filter(training_sentences %in% c(500L, 2000L)) |>
  summarise(
    points = diff(accuracy) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pull(points)

training_ratio_100_to_500 <- 500L / 100L
training_ratio_500_to_2000 <- 2000L / 500L

accuracy_summary <- scored |>
  summarise(
    held_out_tokens = n(),
    lookup_correct = sum(baseline_correct),
    lookup_accuracy = lookup_correct / held_out_tokens,
    tagger_correct = sum(tagger_correct),
    tagger_accuracy = tagger_correct / held_out_tokens,
    gain_points = (tagger_accuracy - lookup_accuracy) * 100,
    seen_tokens = sum(seen_in_training),
    seen_percent = seen_tokens / held_out_tokens * 100,
    easy_tokens = sum(easy_gold_tag),
    easy_percent = easy_tokens / held_out_tokens * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

content_summary <- scored |>
  filter(!easy_gold_tag) |>
  summarise(
    held_out_tokens = n(),
    lookup_correct = sum(baseline_correct),
    lookup_accuracy = lookup_correct / held_out_tokens,
    tagger_correct = sum(tagger_correct),
    tagger_accuracy = tagger_correct / held_out_tokens,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

accuracy_comparison <- tibble(
  scope = c(
    "All held-out tokens",
    "All held-out tokens",
    "Excluding PUNCT and DET",
    "Excluding PUNCT and DET"
  ),
  system = c(
    "Lookup baseline",
    "500-sentence tagger",
    "Lookup baseline",
    "500-sentence tagger"
  ),
  correct = c(
    accuracy_summary$lookup_correct,
    accuracy_summary$tagger_correct,
    content_summary$lookup_correct,
    content_summary$tagger_correct
  ),
  tokens = c(
    accuracy_summary$held_out_tokens,
    accuracy_summary$held_out_tokens,
    content_summary$held_out_tokens,
    content_summary$held_out_tokens
  ),
  accuracy = round(correct / tokens, 4)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  learning_curve_display,
  col.names = c(
    "Training sentences",
    "Training tokens",
    "Held-out tokens",
    "Correct tokens",
    "Accuracy",
    "Accuracy percent"
  ),
  caption = "Held-out tagger accuracy as training data increases",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  accuracy_comparison,
  col.names = c("Tokens included", "System", "Correct", "Tokens", "Accuracy"),
  caption = "The 500-sentence tagger compared with a lookup baseline",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(length(train_newdoc_ids), 11L),
  identical(length(held_newdoc_ids), 13L),
  all(str_starts(train_newdoc_ids, "weblog-")),
  all(str_starts(held_newdoc_ids, "weblog-")),
  identical(range(treebank_years), c(2003L, 2006L)),
  identical(scored_500$correct_tokens, 3641L),
  identical(scored_500$held_out_tokens, 4007L),
  identical(round(scored_500$calculated_accuracy, 4), 0.9087),
  identical(round(accuracy_summary$lookup_accuracy, 4), 0.7931),
  identical(accuracy_summary$lookup_correct, 3178L),
  identical(accuracy_summary$tagger_correct, 3641L),
  identical(accuracy_summary$seen_tokens, 3140L),
  identical(round(accuracy_summary$seen_percent, 1), 78.4),
  identical(accuracy_summary$easy_tokens, 884L),
  identical(round(accuracy_summary$easy_percent, 1), 22.1),
  identical(content_summary$held_out_tokens, 3123L),
  identical(content_summary$tagger_correct, 2766L),
  identical(round(content_summary$tagger_accuracy, 4), 0.8857),
  identical(content_summary$lookup_correct, 2307L),
  identical(round(content_summary$lookup_accuracy, 4), 0.7387),
  identical(round(accuracy_summary$gain_points, 1), 11.6),
  identical(round(gain_100_to_500, 1), 8.5),
  identical(round(gain_500_to_2000, 1), 3.4),
  identical(training_ratio_100_to_500, 5),
  identical(training_ratio_500_to_2000, 4)
)
```

The lookup baseline assigns each word its most frequent tag from the 500
training sentences. It assigns `NOUN` to unseen words.
It correctly tags 3,178 of 4,007 tokens, or 0.7931.
The trained tagger correctly tags 3,641 of 4,007, or about 91 percent.
This is about 11.6 points above the lookup baseline.

Of the 4,007 held-out tokens, 3,140 also appear in the training sentences.
Those tokens account for 78.4 percent of the held-out set.

The easier tags `PUNCT` and `DET` account for 884 of 4,007 held-out tokens, or
22.1 percent. Without them, the trained tagger scores 2,766 of 3,123, or
0.8857. The lookup baseline scores 2,307 of 3,123, or 0.7387.
The easier tokens increase both overall scores.

On this learning curve, accuracy increases quickly at first and then more
slowly. Increasing training from 100 to 500 sentences adds about 8.5 points.
Increasing from 500 to 2,000 adds about 3.4 points.
Each step adds blog posts and sentences, so the curve cannot separate training
quantity from topic coverage. The intervals also differ proportionally.
The first is a five-fold increase, and the second is a four-fold increase.

## Keep the limits attached

The score comes from one run over thirteen blog posts.
Tokens within a post are not independent because they share vocabulary, topic,
and author. Actual variation exceeds what the token count alone suggests.
The builder script sets `set.seed(20260828)`.

The RNG and R-version rows describe the current environment, not the committed
model's build-time environment. This page reports only the bundled run.
It provides no confidence interval because it neither retrains nor rescores
on new samples or domains.

The Riverton text contains job postings and flyer lines, a different type of
writing. This lesson does not claim the same accuracy there.
It shows individual Riverton mistakes that readers can evaluate.

Universal POS tags provide grammatical categories for this task. Other projects can
choose a different tagset.

## What to remember

- A part-of-speech tagger assigns a grammatical tag to each token.
- Universal POS tags are compact labels such as `NOUN`, `VERB`, and `ADJ`.
- The local tagger labeled 178 Riverton tokens.
- Its held-out weblog-post accuracy is 3,641 of 4,007 tokens, or about 91
  percent.
- Examine job-posting errors directly.
- Weblog-post accuracy does not establish job-posting accuracy.

The team can use the tagger to make a first action-word list, then examine the
mistakes before treating the labels as evidence.
